clue.text: Do put on nut in part of engine

indicators.note: one piece is placed onto the end of another, so the first word named here comes second

parts.note: a nut or crank is an eccentric person
to do someone is to cheat them, to shaft them

explanation.surface: A mechanic's instruction to fit a nut onto some engine component.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do' looks like an auxiliary verb but means swindle, and 'nut' is a person, not hardware; 'put on' means the swindle word follows.
explanation.definitionFit: The crankshaft is the rotating rod in an engine that converts piston motion into turning motion.

indicators.note: over the telephone a word is only heard, so a soundalike spelling is wanted

parts.note: a site is a location

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether to mention where they are during a call.
explanation.definitionFit: To cite something is to quote or refer to it, a close synonym of mention.

clue.text: Flower beds carried first of tulips in botanical garden

indicators.note: to bed something is to hold or lodge it, so the flower wraps around what follows

parts.note: the arum is a lily-like plant
past tense of bear, to carry

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the following word is wanted

parts.note: first letter of tulips

explanation.surface: Flowerbeds bearing tulips at the front of a botanical garden display.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower beds' reads as garden plots, but the flower ARUM 'beds' BORE and T: AR(BORE T)UM.
explanation.definitionFit: An arboretum is a garden devoted to growing trees for study and display, a kind of botanical collection.

clue.text: Boat that's no different after capsizing?

definitions.text: Boat that's no different after capsizing?

parts.words: Boat that's no different after capsizing?
parts.note: surface reading: a small craft that can roll over and come up unharmed
setter's reading: the boat's name reads the same when turned backwards

explanation.surface: A small craft that rights itself unharmed after rolling over.
explanation.walkthrough: Canoeists in these do roll over and recover, which makes the clue true in both senses; the name is also a palindrome.
explanation.definitionFit: A kayak is a narrow covered canoe paddled with a double-bladed paddle, a small boat that can be rolled upright.

clue.text: Brother unable to speak regarding weapon

parts.note: Harpo was the Marx Brother who never spoke on screen
on means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A sibling who cannot talk is asked about a weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: The Marx Brothers were a US comedy family; Harpo mimed and honked a horn instead of speaking.
explanation.definitionFit: A harpoon is a barbed spear thrown or fired to catch whales and large fish, so it is a weapon.

clue.text: Middle Eastern food, some endlessly in decline

indicators.note: one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: to decline is to fall

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is dropped

parts.note: a few means some

explanation.surface: Middle Eastern cuisine, someone notes, has been slowly falling out of favour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some' stands for a two-word phrase here, and 'endlessly' trims only that phrase, not the decline word around it.
explanation.definitionFit: Falafel are deep-fried balls of ground chickpeas, a staple street food of the Middle East.

definitions.note: read as a noun: an eccentric person

definitions.meaning: second meaning: one of the court ... in a pack

explanation.surface: A monarch with odd habits, offered as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A card is both a playing card such as a king and, informally, a quirky, entertaining person.

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: the indefinite article
a story is a falsehood, a lie

explanation.surface: A newspaper article carries a story from abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'story' means a fib here, not a news report.
explanation.definitionFit: Alien as an adjective means belonging to another country or unfamiliar, the same as foreign.

parts.note: to dog someone is to follow them
to collar someone is to catch or arrest them

explanation.surface: A white strap is fastened after something has been caught.
explanation.walkthrough: 'White straps' is a playful description of clerical collars, the stiff white bands worn by priests.
explanation.definitionFit: Dog collars are the stiff white neckbands of clergy, jokingly described as bands or straps that are white.

parts.note: a tab is a small flap
close by means nearby

explanation.surface: A cat flap that the cat can easily get to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cat flap' looks like one object; 'Cat' is the definition and 'flap' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A tabby is a cat with a striped or mottled coat, so it is a kind of cat.

indicators.note: something criminal is bent or crooked, so the letters are twisted out of order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Letting a felon go free is common practice, someone complains.
explanation.definitionFit: Releasing someone means setting them at liberty, which is what freeing them does.

clue.text: Island in conflict with island, briefly

indicators.note: made short, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: anti means opposed to
Guam is a Pacific island

explanation.surface: One island is at odds with another, in short.
explanation.definitionFit: Antigua is a Caribbean island, part of the nation of Antigua and Barbuda.

clue.text: Playboy out for percentage in unlawful venture?

parts.note: a rake is a dissolute pleasure-seeker
off means away or out, as with a light

explanation.surface: A playboy is excluded from his cut of a shady deal.
explanation.definitionFit: A rake-off is a share of profits, often illicit, skimmed from a deal, so a cut of a crooked enterprise.

indicators.note: one piece comes behind the other in the word

parts.note: to tan someone's hide is to beat them
a go is a move or turn

explanation.surface: A dancer steps off on the beat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beat' looks musical, but here it means thrash.
explanation.definitionFit: The tango is a ballroom dance of Argentine origin with sharp, dramatic steps.

clue.text: Steps taken to defend strike resulting in shiner

indicators.note: defending means standing around and shielding, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: a flight is a set of stairs
to lash is to hit

explanation.surface: A blow struck in self-defence leaves someone with a black eye.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shiner' suggests a black eye from the strike, but here it is literally something that shines: F(LASH)LIGHT.
explanation.definitionFit: A flashlight is a torch, an object that shines, so it is a shiner in the literal sense.

clue.text: After one has gone, relation devastated in the future

indicators.note: something devastated is wrecked, so the letters are scattered into a new order
something that has gone is removed from the word

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: After a death, a family member is left devastated for the time ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: I is removed from RELATION, and the remaining letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Later on is an adverbial phrase meaning at some subsequent time, that is, in the future.

indicators.note: to mould is to shape something anew, so the letters are reshaped

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The leafy top of a carrot stuck fast to some mould.
explanation.definitionFit: Carrot-top is a teasing nickname for a person with ginger or red hair.

clue.text: Joke, cricket shot towards the on side?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a tease, as in pulling someone's leg

definitions.text: cricket shot towards the on side?
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a pull shot hit to the leg side

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the leg side is also called the on side, and a pull is a shot hitting a short ball across to it; the question mark flags the made-up shot name.
explanation.definitionFit: A leg-pull is a playful hoax or tease, an attempt to fool someone in fun.

parts.note: under means below in rank
a flower is something that flows, a river: the Wear in north-east England

explanation.surface: Bloomers are perhaps a lesser kind of flower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomers' and 'flower' both suggest plants; bloomers are baggy knickers and 'flower' is a river.
explanation.definitionFit: Bloomers are loose old-fashioned knickers, an example of underwear, hence 'perhaps'.

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: say, as in 'take, say, ten' means perhaps or for example

indicators.note: going back means reading the word from the end

parts.note: a protest march is a demo

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether the soldiers might eventually march back in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'march' is the protest kind, and 'perhaps' stands for the word used to offer an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Someday means at some unspecified future time, much as eventually does.

clue.text: Fairish call over leaders in organisation waiting years

indicators.note: in a down answer, over means placed above, so this piece comes first

parts.note: to call loudly is to yell

indicators.note: the leaders of words are their first letters

parts.note: first letters of organisation and waiting
Y is the abbreviation for years

explanation.surface: A complaint that a big organisation keeps people waiting for years.
explanation.definitionFit: Yellowy means tending to yellow; fair hair is pale yellow, so fairish is a fair description.

parts.note: mean means nasty or malicious

indicators.note: something returning goes back the way it came, so it is read backwards

parts.note: cardinal is a deep red, the colour of cardinals' robes

explanation.surface: A wicked cardinal comes back, and someone cries out at the sight of a snake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'snake' is a verb here, to wind about, not the reptile.
explanation.definitionFit: To meander is to follow a winding course, which is what a road or river does when it snakes.

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: Americans say math where Britons say maths
a gong is a medal or honour, such as the CBE

explanation.surface: Someone plays a gong inside an American's study.
explanation.walkthrough: CBE (Commander of the Order of the British Empire) is a British honour, informally a gong: MA(CBE)TH.
explanation.definitionFit: Macbeth is Shakespeare's tragedy about a Scottish usurper, so it is a play.

parts.note: laps as a verb means drinks, as a cat does

indicators.note: only the final letter of the following word is wanted

parts.note: the last letter of bottle

explanation.surface: A failure turns to the bottle and drinks it to the dregs.
explanation.definitionFit: A lapse is a slip or a failure, as in a lapse of concentration.
Plain can mean sheer or absolute and also undecorated or uncomplicated.

indicators.note: something wicked is twisted, so the letters are turned into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a person who is wicked and cruel is the one meant.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the definition: the Devil is the wicked, cruel one asked about.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucifer is a name for Satan, the fallen angel who embodies wickedness and cruelty.

definitions.note: read as a noun: a lively dance
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a lively Scottish dance

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' and 'reel' suggest fishing; they are separate meanings, a throw and a Scottish dance.
explanation.definitionFit: Fling means to throw hard, and a fling is also a vigorous Highland dance, like a reel.

indicators.note: in a down answer, climbing means going upwards, so the letters read from bottom to top
only some of the following letters are used, a run sitting inside the words

parts.note: letters running across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A question about a mountainous spot worth scaling.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: the range is a mountainous place to climb.
explanation.definitionFit: The Alps are the great mountain range of central Europe, famous for climbing and skiing.

clue.text: Epic ego is out to steal foreign money

indicators.note: stealing takes something in, so the rearranged letters take in another piece
out can mean wrong or disordered, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
the rand is the currency of South Africa

explanation.surface: An enormous ego sets out to pocket some foreign cash.
explanation.walkthrough: The rand is South Africa's currency; it sits inside the rearranged letters, just after their first.
explanation.definitionFit: Grandiose means impressively grand in scale or ambition, which is what epic suggests.

indicators.note: what someone might say is spoken, so a soundalike is wanted

parts.note: a croupier at a card table announces that they deal the cards

explanation.surface: The perfect line for a casino croupier to say.
explanation.walkthrough: A croupier runs a casino gaming table; at cards the croupier would say 'I deal'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ideal means perfect, the best that could be imagined.

indicators.note: the phrase houses the answer, holding it inside its letters

parts.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: A river runs quite close to some homes.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tyne is the river flowing through Newcastle in north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tyne is a river in north-east England, flowing out to the North Sea.

indicators.note: something murdered is mangled or destroyed, so these letters are broken up and reformed

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A plea to pray as a Goth invader kills a philosopher.
explanation.definitionFit: Pythagoras was an ancient Greek philosopher and mathematician, best known for his theorem on right triangles.
